narrative:
The model estimates you have a 49% chance of leaving your job, which is high enough that the company has decided to deny your promotion to reduce the risk of investing in someone who might soon depart.

The prediction is driven primarily by three key factors, ranked by importance. First, your total years of experience across all jobs had the strongest influence, but it pulled the prediction toward staying rather than leaving. With only 1-5 years overall, you are in the most common group among employees the model expects to remain, so this actually worked in your favor.

What pushed the prediction toward leaving was, second, that you have received other job offers while working here. This is relatively uncommon—only 23% of employees predicted to stay reported receiving outside opportunities—making it a clear signal that you may be considering alternatives.

Third, although you feel you have received the promotions you deserved in this role, this factor still nudged the outcome slightly toward leaving. Among those the model expects to stay, a higher share report not getting their deserved promotions, so your positive experience here was less decisive than the other signals.

The organization should discuss your career goals openly with you and explore whether additional responsibilities or adjustments could increase your commitment. You may want to reflect on how those external opportunities align with your long-term plans before making any decisions. (218 words)
